title: Forces, Matter and Cells
intro: Gravity, particles, cells and the science of everyday things.

questions.prompt: Which state of matter keeps a fixed shape?
questions.explanation: In a solid, the particles are held tightly in place, so a solid keeps its shape.

questions.prompt: At sea level, pure water boils at what temperature?
questions.explanation: At normal air pressure, pure water boils at 100 °C and freezes at 0 °C.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the force that pulls objects towards Earth?
questions.explanation: Gravity is a non-contact force that pulls objects with mass towards each other, so things fall to the ground.

questions.prompt: What unit is force measured in?
questions.explanation: Force is measured in newtons (N), named after the scientist Isaac Newton.

questions.prompt: What is the basic building block of all living things?
questions.explanation: All living things are made of cells, the smallest units of life.

questions.prompt: Which part of a cell controls its activities and holds its genetic material?
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains genetic material and controls what happens in the cell.

questions.prompt: Sound can travel through empty space, where there is no air.
questions.explanation: Sound needs particles to vibrate, so it cannot travel through a vacuum. Light can.

questions.prompt: What is the chemical formula for water?
questions.explanation: Each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, so its formula is H₂O.

questions.prompt: Which of these metals is attracted to a magnet?
questions.explanation: Iron is a magnetic metal. Copper, aluminium and gold are not attracted to magnets.

questions.prompt: What is it called when a liquid turns into a gas at its surface?
questions.explanation: Evaporation is when particles escape from the surface of a liquid and become a gas.

questions.prompt: In which part of a plant cell does photosynthesis take place?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain green chlorophyll, which traps light energy so the plant can make glucose.

questions.prompt: Which part of a plant cell is filled with cell sap and helps keep the cell firm?
questions.explanation: The permanent vacuole stores cell sap. When it is full of water it pushes outwards, keeping the plant cell firm.

questions.prompt: Which of these is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a tough cell wall made of cellulose that gives them strength. Animal cells do not have one.

questions.prompt: Plant cells and animal cells both have a nucleus.
questions.explanation: Both kinds of cell have a nucleus, cytoplasm and a cell membrane. The differences are extras like the cell wall and chloroplasts.

questions.prompt: What is the job of the cell membrane?

options.label: It controls what goes into and out of the cell
It stores the cell's genetic material

questions.explanation: The cell membrane is a thin barrier around the cell that lets some substances in and out but keeps others back.

questions.prompt: A cyclist travels 100 metres in 5 seconds. What is her average speed in metres per second?
questions.explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time, so 100 m ÷ 5 s = 20 metres per second.

questions.prompt: Which formula is used to work out pressure?
questions.explanation: Pressure is force divided by area. That is why a sharp knife, with a tiny area, cuts more easily than a blunt one.

questions.prompt: Which statement about mass and weight is correct?

options.label: Weight is a force caused by gravity, but mass is the amount of matter
Mass is a force measured in newtons
Mass and weight are exactly the same thing
Your weight is the same on every planet

questions.explanation: Mass is measured in kilograms and stays the same everywhere. Weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons.

questions.prompt: An astronaut has the same mass on the Moon as on Earth.
questions.explanation: Mass does not change with location. The astronaut weighs less on the Moon only because the Moon's gravity is weaker.

questions.prompt: Which force acts against motion when two surfaces rub together?
questions.explanation: Friction acts in the opposite direction to movement. It helps shoes grip the ground but also slows moving things down.

questions.prompt: A moving object has balanced forces acting on it. What happens to its motion?

options.label: It keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction

questions.explanation: Balanced forces cancel out, so they cause no change in motion. Only an unbalanced force can speed up, slow down or turn an object.

questions.prompt: Which of these substances is a compound?
questions.explanation: A compound contains two or more elements chemically joined. Carbon dioxide is made of carbon and oxygen atoms bonded together.

questions.prompt: A solution has a pH of exactly 7. What is it?
questions.explanation: On the pH scale, below 7 is acidic, above 7 is alkaline and exactly 7 is neutral, like pure water.

questions.prompt: What is the reaction between an acid and an alkali that makes a salt and water called?
questions.explanation: In neutralisation the acid and alkali cancel each other out, producing a salt and water.

questions.prompt: What is the name for particles spreading out from where there are lots of them to where there are fewer?
questions.explanation: Diffusion is why the smell of toast spreads across a kitchen: particles move from high to low concentration.

questions.prompt: At sea level, at what temperature in °C does pure water freeze?
questions.explanation: Pure water freezes, and ice melts, at 0 °C. Adding salt lowers this temperature, which is why salt is spread on icy roads.

questions.prompt: Light travels faster than sound.
questions.explanation: Light is about a million times faster than sound in air. That is why you see lightning before you hear the thunder.

questions.prompt: What do we call it when light bounces off a mirror?
questions.explanation: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface. Smooth, shiny surfaces like mirrors reflect light very evenly.

questions.prompt: The particles in a solid do not move at all.
questions.explanation: Particles in a solid are held in fixed positions, but they still vibrate. Heating makes them vibrate more.

questions.prompt: Which of these metals is the most reactive?
questions.explanation: Potassium is near the top of the reactivity series and reacts violently with water. Gold is near the bottom and hardly reacts at all.
